title: Room-by-room deep-clean execution and sequencing
audience: Bond and end-of-lease cleaners running a room-by-room deep clean.
referencesAtStart: Official sources: Safe Work Australia, Lifting, pushing and pulling (manual tasks) (no date shown); Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC), Small business and the Privacy Act (published 10 March 2023; last modified 5 September 2024); Safe Work Australia, Hazardous chemicals register (no date shown); Safe Work Australia, National guide for working with silica and silica containing products (February 2022).
learningOutcomes: Prepare the site and a clean equipment staging area before starting.
Sequence the work high-to-low and dry-remove dust before wet processes.
Check each zone against its acceptance criteria before moving on.

instruction.heading: Preparing the site
instruction.body:
Before the first cloth is wet, confirm the basics of the property. Check access to the building and to each room, the position of the power, water and gas controls, and the ventilation that is available. Walk the property with the agreed scope and note any hazards: loose floor coverings, wet or slippery areas, damaged electrical fittings, fragile glass, pest activity, and any product or chemical left by the occupant. Record the surface condition as you find it, room by room, so that a later question about a mark or a chip can be answered from the record. The record is the baseline for the whole job.

Photograph pre-existing issues only with the permission of the occupant or the owner, and only within the privacy rules that apply to your business. The federal Privacy Act generally does not apply to a business with an annual turnover of $3 million or less, but it does apply to some small businesses regardless of turnover, including health service providers and businesses that trade in personal information. Check your own position before you rely on the exemption (OAIC, small business page; last modified 5 September 2024). Keep photographs focused on the surfaces and fixtures, and avoid personal papers and belongings.

Set up a clean equipment staging area near the entry, outside the path of the work. Place the cloths, buckets, products and the vacuum there, with the SDS for each product in a folder on site. Keep products on a tray or trolley rather than on the floor, and keep the staging area separate from the dirty water and used cloths. A staging area that sits in the middle of a room gets knocked over, and a spill from a product on the floor can cause a slip or a contaminated surface.

instruction.heading: Sequence: high to low, and dust before water
instruction.body:
Work high to low, and from less soiled to more soiled where practicable. Start with the high points: light fittings and covers, ceiling fan blades and the tops of wall units, then the upper walls and door frames, then the windows and sills, then the lower walls, the fixtures and the cupboard fronts, and finally the floors. Floors are cleaned last where it is safe to do so, because the dust and drips from above fall onto them. A team that cleans floors first and then removes overhead dust creates rework, and the sequence must change.

Dry-remove loose dust before any wet process, so that the dust does not turn into a film or mud. Use a dry cloth, a dusting tool or an approved vacuum with a suitable filter. Where the dust may contain crystalline silica, which can come from concrete, grout, stone or tile, the national guide on silica states that dry sweeping, compressed air and general-purpose vacuums must not be used to clean dusty surfaces. It recommends wet methods, low-pressure water, wet sweeping or a vacuum of the class the guide describes. It also warns that handheld spray bottles and sponges are not adequate for suppressing silica dust, so a dusty surface that contains silica needs the controls in the guide, not a quick wipe. Check the SDS or the supplier's data before you decide that a dust does not contain silica.

Protect completed areas from recontamination. Close a finished room, or mark it with a clear sign and a boundary, so that the team does not walk back through it with dirty shoes or equipment. Work from the far end of a room towards the exit, so that you do not step on finished areas.

instruction.heading: Kitchens, bathrooms and fixtures
instruction.body: In bathrooms, clean from the top down: fan covers and vents, the shower head and the screens, the walls and tiles, the basin, the bath, the toilet, and then the floor. Use dedicated sanitary cloths and tools for the bathroom only, and keep them out of the kitchen and the living areas. Apply product to the cloth, rather than spraying it into fittings, and follow the product's dwell and rinse instructions. Protect finishes that a product can dull or mark, and test a product on an inconspicuous area first. In kitchens, clean from the top down as well, and clean the surfaces that food touches with a product that the label says is suitable for that purpose. Clean inside cupboards and drawers that are empty, and keep residue out of the stored items. Do not disassemble an appliance to clean behind or inside it. Clean the accessible parts, note what you could not reach, and report it. Moving furniture, appliances and heavy fittings is a manual task. Identify the items that need moving before the clean starts, and remove the hazard where you can, for example by agreeing that the occupant empties a cupboard before you arrive. Where the item must move, reduce the risk with a mechanical aid, a change to the layout, a second person where the item needs it, and training. Safe Work Australia states that the business must identify and manage the risk of manual tasks, and that elimination comes first, followed by ways to minimise the risk that remains (Safe Work Australia, lifting, pushing and pulling manual tasks; no date shown). Stay within the agreed scope, and check every zone against its acceptance criteria before you move on.

instruction.heading: Zone sign-off before moving on
instruction.body: Each zone is checked against its acceptance criteria before the team moves to the next one. The criteria are written before the work starts, and they name the surfaces, the fixtures and the standard expected for each. Check the zone under a good light, from the doorway and from close up, because a room can look clean from one position and still have missed cleaning behind a fixture or in a corner. Mark the zone as signed off only when every criterion is met, or record the item that is not met and why. Where a mark or a stain remains after the approved method, record it as unresolved, with a photograph where permitted, and note that it was not removed by the method used. Do not describe an unresolved mark as cleaned.

procedure: Confirm access, utilities, ventilation, hazards, surface condition and zones, and record the baseline room by room.
Photograph pre-existing issues only with permission, and keep the photographs within the privacy rules that apply.
Set up a clean equipment staging area outside the path of the work, with the SDS for each product on site.
Work high to low and less soiled to more soiled, and dry-remove dust before any wet process.
Where dust may contain silica, use the wet or approved-vacuum methods in the silica guide, and never dry sweep or use compressed air.
Clean bathrooms and kitchens with dedicated tools, follow product dwell and rinse instructions, and do not disassemble appliances.
Identify manual tasks in advance, remove the hazard where possible, and use mechanical aids and a second person where the item needs it.
Check each zone against its acceptance criteria before moving on, and record any unresolved marks.

workedExamples.situation: A team cleans the floors first and then removes overhead dust from the light fittings and the top of the wall unit, creating rework.
workedExamples.reasoning: Re-sequence the job so that dust from high surfaces is removed first, then the wet work, with floors last. Add a zone sign-off so that each area is checked before the team moves on. Record the change in the job's sequence so that the next team follows the same order. The rework is a sequencing error, not a fault of the product used.

workedExamples.situation: A heavy sofa must be moved so that the skirting board behind it can be cleaned, and the occupant is not present to help.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How is the manual task handled before anyone lifts?
workedExamples.reasoning: Identify the sofa as a manual task before the clean starts. Ask whether the occupant can move it or whether it can stay in place with the skirting cleaned only where it is reachable. If it must move, use a mechanical aid, such as a sliding device or a trolley, rather than lifting it alone, and use a second person. Record the area that could not be reached and the reason, and report it to the supervisor. Do not lift the sofa alone to finish the job.

workedExamples.situation: The oven door has a baked-on residue around the seal, and the team wants to take the door off to clean behind it.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not remove the door or disassemble the oven without training and the occupant's agreement. Clean the accessible parts of the oven with the approved product and follow its dwell and rinse instructions. Record the residue that could not be reached, with a photograph where permitted, and report it as an unresolved item in the zone sign-off.

equipmentAndPpe: Dedicated sanitary tools and cloths, kept separate from kitchen and living area tools.
Approved products, each with its label and SDS on site.
Vacuum with a filter suited to the dust, as the silica guide describes where silica may be present.
Gloves and eye protection as set by the SDS and the risk assessment.
Respiratory protection where the dust or the product requires it, as set by the risk assessment and the SDS.
Mechanical aids for moving furniture, such as sliders or a trolley, and a second person where an item needs it.
Inspection light and the zone sign-off sheet with the acceptance criteria.

commonErrors.prevention: Dry-remove dust first, using a dry cloth, a dusting tool or an approved vacuum.

commonErrors.error: Cleaning floors before the overhead surfaces.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean high to low, with floors last where safe.

commonErrors.error: Using compressed air or dry sweeping on dusty surfaces that may contain silica.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the wet methods or the approved vacuum in the silica guide, and check the SDS or supplier data for silica.

commonErrors.error: Disassembling an appliance to clean behind it.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean only the accessible parts, and record and report the rest.

commonErrors.error: Lifting heavy furniture alone to reach a skirting board.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify the manual task first, use a mechanical aid or a second person, and record any area not reached.

commonErrors.error: Leaving the staging area in the path of the work.
commonErrors.prevention: Set up the staging area outside the path of the work, on a tray or trolley off the floor.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The business is responsible for managing the risk of musculoskeletal injury from manual tasks. It must identify the hazardous tasks and assess and manage the risks so far as is reasonably practicable. The Safe Work Australia page places elimination first, then changes to design and layout, workspace heights, redesigned tasks such as mechanical aids, rotation of tasks between workers, and training (no date shown).

Whether the Privacy Act covers photographs taken during a clean depends on the business. Most businesses with an annual turnover of $3 million or less are outside the Act, but some small businesses are covered regardless of turnover, including health service providers and businesses that trade in personal information (OAIC, small business page; last modified 5 September 2024).

Chemicals used on a job must be managed under the label and the SDS. A hazardous chemicals register kept at the workplace must list the current SDS for each listed chemical, and it must be readily accessible to workers and others who may be affected (Safe Work Australia, hazardous chemicals register page; no date shown).

Dust that may contain crystalline silica must be controlled with the methods in the national silica guide. The guide states that workers must never use compressed air, dry sweeping or a general-purpose vacuum to clean dusty surfaces, and that wet methods alone may not adequately control high-silica dust (Safe Work Australia, national guide for working with silica, February 2022).
Product-specific dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the product label and SDS.

qualityStandard: The site is prepared, the baseline is recorded, and the staging area is set before the simulated clean.
The sequence is followed high to low, with dust removed before wet work and floors last, in the simulation.
Dust that may contain silica is handled with the wet or approved-vacuum method, with no dry sweeping or compressed air.
Each zone is checked against its acceptance criteria and signed off, or the unresolved item is recorded, before the team moves on.
documentationEvidence: Baseline condition record, room by room, with the permitted photographs.
Zone sign-off record against the acceptance criteria, with the date and the name of the person checking.
Record of unresolved marks, surface damage and any area not reached, with photographs where permitted.
Record of any manual task and the control used, such as a mechanical aid or a second person.
summary: Prepare the site, record the baseline, and set up the staging area outside the path of the work.
Work high to low, dry-remove dust before wet work, and clean floors last, using the silica guide where silica may be present.
Sign off each zone against its criteria before moving on, and record anything that remains.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is dry dust removed before any wet cleaning?
options: Otherwise the dust turns to mud or a film and creates rework
It is faster to do it later, once the room is empty
Wet cleaning does not pick up dust, so the order does not matter
It does not matter in what order the work is done

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the usual order for a room?
options: Floors first, then the high surfaces
High to low, with floors last where safe
Walls last, after the floors are dry

knowledgeChecks.question: When can a zone be marked as finished?
options: When it looks finished from the doorway, since the room looks clean at a glance to the owner
When the time allowed for the room has run out, even if some items remain open for the job
When it meets its acceptance criteria and is signed off, or the unresolved items are recorded
When the occupant says it is good enough, without any sign-off from the supervisor
